title: Twelve small books
hookLine: twelve short prophets, written together on one scroll

lines: SHORT ENOUGH FOR A BUS RIDE.
cards: How do you keep a small book from getting lost? Isaiah, Jeremiah and Ezekiel each fill a long book of their own. After them come twelve more prophets, and some of their books are short enough to read on a bus ride.
A herdsman from Tekoa. A man who ran from God by ship. A prophet who spoke against one neighboring nation, Edom.
Instead of twelve little scrolls, tradition wrote them end to end, on one.

teach.b: Trei Asar. It's Aramaic, and it simply means twelve. Not the minor prophets.
Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi. Said out loud, it sounds like a class roll call. So why one scroll?
The Talmud, in tractate Bava Batra, asks about the order of the prophets.

Near the start of Hosea's book come the words, the beginning of the word of the LORD by Hosea, and the rabbis take that to mean his prophecy came early. Then why isn't his book placed before Isaiah? Their answer is plain.

teach.h: BECAUSE IT IS SMALL, IT MIGHT GET LOST.
teach.b: Hosea is written together with the last prophets, Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi, and because his book is small, it might get lost. A short scroll can slip behind a shelf.
Twelve, sewn into one, stay found: a kind of protection for the quiet ones. And they're quiet only on the outside. Inside: a prophet whose broken marriage becomes a picture of God and Israel.
A prophet who asks for justice to well up as waters. A runaway swallowed by a great fish. Lines still read aloud in synagogue.
In the Talmud's list of the prophets, the Twelve appear under that one name, as a single book.

teach.h: BOUND IN WITH OTHERS, THEY LAST.
teach.b: That's how a small voice lasts: not alone, but bound in with others. Over the next stretch of days, this path walks through the scroll, one prophet at a time.

how: In Jewish Bibles the twelve short prophets, Hosea through Malachi, are grouped as one book called Trei Asar, and passages from them are read as haftarot in synagogue.

o: the scroll of the twelve short prophets, as one book
the twelve tribes named in the blessing of Jacob
a set of twelve laws the rabbis drew from the Torah

games.q: small books, big voices — tap the pairs.
p: small, so it might get lost
where the rabbis discuss the order

s: the twelve are grouped together because their words matter less
they're grouped because the books are short. the voices inside are anything but small.
trei asar is Aramaic, and simply means twelve
the name is just the number: the Twelve.
the Talmud worries a small book might get lost on its own
that's the reason Bava Batra gives for Hosea being written with the others.

games.q: you're a scribe holding twelve short books of prophecy. what do you do with them?
o: give each its own little scroll.
write them together on one scroll.
games.why: tradition wrote them end to end on one scroll. the Talmud says a small book alone could get lost.

practice: If there's a Bible or a reading app nearby, open to any of the Twelve and read one short chapter slowly, start to finish, with no study notes, just the words.
If you'd rather not read right now, say the twelve names once, slowly, and let one of them stay with you. If you pray, you can ask to hear one small voice clearly.

wordCard.voice: Trei Asar. Aramaic for twelve: the twelve short prophets, written together on one scroll so none of them would be lost. Today's word.

orig.note: Aramaic: twelve, the name for the scroll of the twelve short prophets.
